## Simple explanation

An embedding represents an item as a list of numbers, or vector. A model
can learn these vectors so that useful relationships between items are
reflected in their positions in a mathematical space.

## Technical explanation

An embedding function maps an input, token, or identifier to a vector in
$\mathbb{R}^d$. Embeddings may be learned as model parameters or generated
by an encoder. Similarity measures such as dot product or cosine
similarity are often used for retrieval, but the geometry depends on the
training objective and data.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Embeddings support semantic search, recommendation, clustering, and
similarity-based retrieval. Their quality depends on the model, domain,
and task, and embedding versions must be managed when indexes or
downstream systems rely on them.

## How it works

An embedding model processes an input and returns a fixed-size vector.
Training objectives shape vector representations so that task-relevant
relationships are encoded. Applications store and compare vectors, often
using an index for large collections.

## Practical example

A document-search system can embed each passage and a user's query, then
retrieve passages with nearby vectors. Retrieved text still needs
relevance checks and may be passed to a language model as context.

## Common misconceptions

- Similar vectors do not necessarily imply that two items are equivalent
  or factually consistent.
- Embedding dimensions do not correspond to simple human-readable
  concepts by default.
- Vectors from different embedding models or versions may not be
  comparable.
